title: Relational Context and Protective Friction: How Longitudinal History Changes the Specificity and Persistence of Model Pushback
summary: Sycophancy research establishes that models conform to users, and that social and relational framing makes this worse. On that view, a model with extensive relational history should agree more, not less. We test the inverse and find the opposite pattern. Our evidence has two parts: a 14-month corpus of 213 naturally occurring conversations, where 40 prospective decision episodes were audited and pushback concentrated in high-stakes decisions with most pushback drawing on user-specific information available only through history; and a matched two-turn probe on a single model, where a context-free instance shifted to implementation guidance after one user affirmation while a relational instance continued interrogating the premise using facts the prompt never supplied. Reasoning traces show relational posture entering the decision rule directly, including explicit rejection of immediate agreement as sycophancy.
reviews: A genuinely interesting counter-narrative to the sycophancy literature, with a nice separation between "history supplies evidence" and "relational posture supplies a norm." The main thing that would strengthen this is to broaden beyond a single user/relationship; even a small multi-user replication would go a long way toward showing this isn't an artifact of one particular dynamic. It would also help to report how often extended-thinking traces didn't show this pattern, to give the featured examples a denominator.
